claims.text: Reliable formation of noble metal–based HEA nanomaterials is governed by atomic-scale mixing promoted by high-temperature reducing annealing.
High-temperature reducing annealing minimizes oxidation.
High-temperature reducing annealing minimizes phase segregation.
A uniform distribution of noble metals creates synergistic interactions at catalytic active sites.
The proposed treatment is annealing at approximately 500 °C under H2 for approximately 2 hours with controlled cooling.
A predominantly reducing environment prevents oxidation during alloying.
Atomic mixing and alloy homogeneity are reflected in a uniform elemental distribution.
Atomic mixing and alloy homogeneity produce a consistent local electronic structure at active sites.
Thermal energy and low oxygen chemical potential drive complete atomic diffusion and mixing.
Complete atomic diffusion and mixing occur without promoting oxidation under the proposed conditions.
A homogeneous alloy structure enhances electron-cloud overlap among noble metals.
Enhanced electron-cloud overlap reduces catalytic activation barriers.
Materials treated at approximately 500 °C under H2 will have a more uniform elemental distribution than materials treated at lower temperature or under mildly oxidizing conditions.
Materials treated at approximately 500 °C under H2 will exhibit higher turnover frequency than the baseline materials.
Lower-temperature or oxidizing annealing causes incomplete atomic mixing.
Lower-temperature or oxidizing annealing causes partial oxidation and phase segregation.
Incomplete mixing, partial oxidation, and phase segregation reduce catalytic efficiency.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to HEA systems containing four to seven noble-metal elements under sufficiently reducing conditions.
The hypothesis may not apply when constituent metals are highly prone to oxidation.
The hypothesis may not apply to compositions that inherently phase-segregate even under reductive annealing.
